title: Active-Passive
subtitle: Primary-standby replication, monotonic fencing tokens, and mitigating split-brain risk.
keyTakeaways: Active-passive directs all writes to a single primary while replicating state to one or more standbys, preserving strict transactional guarantees without write conflict resolution code.

Split-brain is the primary operational danger: if network partitions isolate the primary, an automated failover can spawn two primaries simultaneously unless protected by consensus leases and fencing tokens.
Passive standbys carry hidden cold-start risks: caches are empty, connection pools are unprimed, and untested failover scripts often fail during real 3 AM emergencies.

                     v                               v
           +---------------------------------------------------+
           | Shared Storage / Downstream Consumer              |
           | Max Seen Epoch = 43 -> REJECTS Epoch #42 (Fenced) |
           +---------------------------------------------------+

sections.heading: Primary-Standby Replication and Fencing Tokens
sections.body: In an active-passive setup, a single primary processes all mutations and streams its Write-Ahead Log (WAL) or replication log to passive standby instances. If the primary crashes, a standby is promoted to become the new primary.
bullets: The split-brain hazard: Suppose Primary A loses network connectivity to the standby cluster due to a temporary switch failure, but can still reach clients. If the monitoring system promotes Standby B to become the new Primary, both instances accept writes simultaneously, corrupting data integrity irreversibly.

Fencing tokens: To prevent split-brain writes, modern consensus systems (ZooKeeper, etcd, Raft) issue a strictly monotonic epoch number or fencing token on every leader election. Stateful backends or storage volumes reject any write bearing an older epoch number than the highest token observed.

Consensus-driven promotion: Never rely on a single external health checker to trigger failovers. Require a quorum of independent consensus nodes (e.g., 3 or 5 nodes) to agree that the primary is unreachable before initiating promotion.

sections.heading: Failure Detection Windows, DNS Caching, and Cold Standby Realities
sections.body: The total recovery time (RTO) in an active-passive architecture equals the time to detect the failure, plus the time to promote the standby, plus the time for client traffic to redirect to the new endpoint.
bullets: Tuning detection timeouts: Setting a heartbeat timeout too aggressively (e.g., 2 seconds) causes spurious failovers during temporary GC pauses or minor network blips. Setting it too conservatively (e.g., 60 seconds) extends user-visible downtime during actual hardware crashes.

Client DNS caching: Updating a DNS record to point to the new standby fails if intermediate resolvers or client runtimes ignore the DNS TTL. Use virtual IP (VIP) failovers or reverse proxy re-routing rather than public DNS whenever low RTO is required.

The cold-cache shock: When a standby is promoted after running idle, its local caches (Redis, Postgres buffer cache) are cold. The sudden wave of diverted production traffic causes severe latency spikes and connection pool exhaustion unless pre-warmed.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero data loss (RPO = 0); strict serializability without complex application conflict resolution.
tradeOffs.cons: Primary write latency pays the network round-trip cost to the standby; standby node sits largely idle, incurring hardware costs.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Core transactional ledgers, relational billing systems, and regulatory financial data.

tradeOffs.pros: Fast local write latency on the primary; primary remains available even if the standby network link degrades temporarily.
tradeOffs.cons: Failover involves a non-zero RPO (a few seconds of committed transactions in the WAL stream can be lost or require manual reconciliation).
tradeOffs.bestFor: General web applications, content management systems, and high-throughput social platforms.

interviewTip: When discussing database failover in an interview, address split-brain directly. Explain how monotonic fencing tokens (or generation IDs) prevent an old, partitioned primary from writing stale records back to storage after a new primary has already been elected.
